# SkillReason: Reasoning-Enhanced Agent Skill Retrieval for Implicit User Requests

- **Authors**: Donghong Jiang, Endian Lin, Luoping Cui, Hanqing Liu, Mingjie Liu, Fan Yang, Hong Wang, Zhao Yang, Chuang Zhu
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-09
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08640>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08640v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-training
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-faithfulness 0.25, reasoning-training 0.40, test-time-scaling 0.25

## In one line

Uses chain-of-thought about required capabilities as training-time supervision for a skill retriever -- distilled from a teacher in stage one and refined by retrieval-rewarded GRPO in stage two -- so that at inference the model encodes the bare query with no generation at all.

## Problem

Agents increasingly draw on libraries of reusable skills, but real user requests are concise and underspecified: they state the goal and leave the required capabilities and execution steps implicit. A retriever matching surface lexical cues therefore has to bridge a semantic gap between a task goal and a skill description. The obvious fix -- have the model reason about what capabilities are needed before retrieving -- destroys the property that makes dense retrieval usable, because autoregressive generation at query time is orders of magnitude more expensive than encoding. Existing benchmarks also cover implicit requests poorly, so the gap was not measurable.

## Contributions

- SkillReason-Bench: 3,729 concise, underspecified cross-domain queries against a shared corpus of 61,228 skills over nine domains, filtered so that confusable alternatives remain distinguishable, with an independent 300-sample two-judge quality audit and a leakage check.
- A stage-I recipe that uses teacher capability-reasoning traces as privileged supervision rather than as inference-time input, combining contrastive learning on both views with a stop-gradient KL that transfers the augmented view's ranking distribution onto the query-only representation.
- Retrieval-guided GRPO in stage II, rewarding sampled reasoning traces by the retrieval margin between the target skill and the strongest negative, so the model explores traces suited to its own capacity rather than imitating one fixed teacher trace.
- The measurement that makes the design worth having: self-generated chain of thought at inference does not beat query-only retrieval from the same checkpoint while costing one to two orders of magnitude in latency, so training-time reasoning supervision is not merely cheaper but as good.
- A sensitivity analysis crediting functionally valid but unannotated alternative skills, showing that single-gold-skill annotation shifts all retrievers by a comparable margin and does not change their ordering.

## Method

Two training stages over an embedding backbone, with a strict constraint that inference stays query-only. Stage I treats a teacher-generated capability reasoning trace c* as privileged supervision available at training but not at test. Four losses are combined: contrastive learning on the original query (which is the path actually used at inference), the same contrastive loss on the augmented query [q; c*], a retrieval distribution alignment term that softens both views' rankings at temperature T and minimises the KL from the privileged augmented view (under stop-gradient) to the query-only view, so the plain query inherits the augmented view's ranking preferences, and a language-modelling loss over the tokens of c* that teaches the shared backbone to generate the trace and thereby initialises a policy for stage II. Stage II replaces the single fixed teacher trace with retrieval-guided GRPO: the stage-I policy samples G capability-reasoning traces per query, a frozen stage-I retriever scores each augmented query by its retrieval margin -- similarity to the target skill minus similarity to the strongest negative -- and the reward is tanh of that margin, so the model explores traces suited to its own capacity rather than imitating one teacher. Benchmark construction is heavily filtered: confusable skills are mined by document overlap and dense retrieval, DeepSeek-R1 keeps only queries whose annotated target stays distinguishable from them, sampling is stratified across nine domains, and DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Haiku 4.5 independently review each query for naturalness, informativeness, capability requirement and target consistency, with disagreements adjudicated by hand. Evaluation covers three benchmarks chosen to differ in how explicit their queries are: SkillReason-Bench (3,729 queries, 61,228 skills, 33.2 words average, implicit), SRA-Bench (5,400 capability-intensive instances over six existing suites, with end-to-end task execution), and SkillRet (4,997 queries, 172.9 words average, long and procedurally explicit, multi-skill).

## Results

SkillReason-0.6B gains 17.56 points of Recall@10 on average over its Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B backbone and beats Qwen3-Embedding-8B on every metric at a thirteenth of the parameters; SkillReason-4B leads most metrics across all three benchmarks (53.58 / 60.90 / 52.03 Recall@1). The cross-benchmark spread is the paper's argument for its own benchmark: SkillRouter and SkillRet retrievers do well on SkillRet, whose queries are long and carry explicit procedural cues, but both fall below a plain Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B on the implicit SkillReason-Bench. Two results cut against the method's own framing and are reported plainly. First, generating a chain of thought at inference and appending it to the query does not beat query-only retrieval from the same checkpoint (44.73 against 45.16 Recall@1 on SkillReason-Bench), while raising mean end-to-end latency from 32.27 ms to 3151.10 ms at 0.6B and from 144.65 ms to 4237.27 ms at 4B -- roughly one to two orders of magnitude for no consistent gain, which the authors read as evidence the reasoning has been internalised. Second, stage-II GRPO helps only where queries are implicit: on SkillRet it regresses the stage-I checkpoint on every metric (Recall@1 53.56 to 52.45, Recall@10 79.32 to 76.70), which the paper attributes to that benchmark's explicit procedural cues and states rather than hides. The stage-I ablation is cumulative and monotone on the implicit benchmarks, with the largest single jump from adding contrastive learning on the CoT-augmented query (35.18 to 39.88 Recall@1). End to end on SRA-Bench, feeding the top-1 retrieved skill to five downstream models raises task accuracy by 14.66 to 25.03 points over no skills and comes close to the gold-skill ceiling (63.84 against 64.23 on Qwen3-4B, 69.09 against 68.84 on Qwen3-32B, where it slightly exceeds it). A diagnostic on SkillBench separates two things the headline conflates: SkillRouter achieves the best Recall@1 on both splits while SkillReason-4B achieves the best full-coverage@10 on multi-skill queries (41.18 Easy, 35.29 Hard), so the gain is in recovering the complete set of complementary skills rather than in ranking one skill first. Latency measurements show reasoning-oriented training adds no online cost -- 31.58 ms against the backbone's 31.69 ms -- while reranking, which does help, costs 1.9 to 4.8 seconds. Two robustness checks support the numbers: an independent quality audit of 300 domain-stratified samples by two judges gives 97.7% joint pass, 98.3% inter-judge agreement and at most 0.33% target leakage; and crediting unannotated but functionally valid alternative skills shifts every retriever by a similar amount (+1.37 to +3.54 Recall@1), leaving the ranking intact.

## Limitations

Stated: the SkillBench multi-skill analysis rests on 75 queries per split and is explicitly treated as diagnostic rather than as a primary result, with conclusions drawn from the larger benchmarks; stage II gives no improvement on procedurally explicit queries and the authors localise its benefit to implicit-query settings; and one audited item is classified as a mild gold-scope mismatch. Not stated but worth noticing: the benchmark is model-mediated at nearly every step -- DeepSeek-R1 filters confusable candidates, DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Haiku 4.5 review queries, teacher traces come from a stronger model, and the 300-sample quality audit is itself performed by Qwen3-235B-A22B and GPT-5.6-Luna -- so 'natural, implicit user request' means what those models judged to be one, and human involvement is confined to adjudicating disagreements. Assigning one official target skill per query in SkillReason-Bench is a known distortion that the authors measure but cannot remove; their sensitivity analysis shows the ranking survives, not that the absolute numbers are right. The end-to-end result uses only the top-1 retrieved skill under direct inference, so nothing is shown about how the retriever behaves inside an agent that can retrieve again after a failure. And the practical recommendation that comes out of the latency table -- spend extra online compute on reranking, not on generating rationales -- rests on rerankers that cost 1.9 to 4.8 seconds per query, which is a different deployment regime from the 32 ms retriever the paper's efficiency argument is built around.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-training**: A well-controlled instance of the pattern this topic keeps circling: training a model with reasoning traces and then not using them at inference. Two measurements make it more than another distillation paper. First, the paper tests the counterfactual its own thesis needs -- take the trained checkpoint and let it generate a capability rationale at query time -- and finds no consistent gain over encoding the bare query (44.73 against 45.16 Recall@1), at 32.27 ms rising to 3151.10 ms. That is direct evidence that what the traces bought was absorbed into the representation rather than into a runtime procedure, and it is the comparison most work claiming 'internalised reasoning' omits. Second, it separates the contributions of the two supervision routes rather than reporting their sum: an explicit KL that transfers the reasoning-augmented view's ranking distribution onto the query-only view is what does the transferring, and the contrastive loss on the augmented query is the single largest step in the stage-I ablation. The stage-II result is the more interesting one for how the archive should read RL-on-top-of-SFT claims. Retrieval-guided GRPO helps where the query is implicit and actively regresses the stage-I checkpoint where the query is long and procedurally explicit (Recall@10 79.32 to 76.70 on SkillRet), and the authors report and localise this rather than averaging it away -- so the benefit of exploring one's own traces over imitating a teacher's is conditional on the task leaving something to infer. Worth carrying forward as a template for the reward too: the RL signal here is not a learned reward model or a judge but a margin between the target and the strongest negative under a frozen retriever, squashed by tanh, which is cheap, verifiable and hard to game. Finally, the SkillBench diagnostic is a useful caution about aggregate metrics: the method that ranks a single annotated skill first is not the one that recovers all the skills a compound request needs, and Recall@1 and full-coverage@10 order the systems differently.

## Abstract

Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to extend their capabilities beyond parametric knowl- edge. However, retrieving the appropriate skill from a large- scale library remains challenging because realistic user re- quests are often concise and underspecified, stating only the task goal while leaving the required capabilities and execu- tion steps implicit. Existing benchmarks provide limited cov- erage of such requests. To address this gap, we introduce SkillReason-Bench, a large-scale cross-domain benchmark containing 3,729 queries and a retrieval corpus of 61,228 skills spanning nine domains. We further propose SkillRea- son, a two-stage framework that uses chain-of-thought rea- soning as training-time supervision for skill retrieval. In Stage I, capability reasoning traces generated by a stronger teacher provide explicit supervision through contrastive learning, re- trieval distribution alignment, and language modeling, en- couraging the retriever to internalize capability reasoning in its query representation. In Stage II, a retrieval-guided GRPO objective encourages the model to explore reasoning trajecto- ries better suited to its own capabilities and more effective for retrieval. At inference, SkillReason directly encodes the orig- inal query without autoregressive CoT generation, preserv- ing efficient query-only retrieval. Extensive experiments on SkillReason-Bench, SkillRet, and SRA-Bench show that Skill- Reason achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three benchmarks, demonstrating that reasoning-enhanced training better bridges the semantic gap between high-level task goals and skill capabilities.
